I	A working man, father of six, sits at the table in his small bungalow on the outskirts of Stoke-
on-Trent in the Midlands of England. He — let’s call him Mr H — takes a pencil and paper and
traces the outline of each of his hands. He then folds the paper and places it, along with a
descriptive note, in an envelope addressed to the Eugenics Society, 20 Grosvenor Gardens,
London, and ‘anxiously awaits reply’.
It is December 1930, and a campaign to legalise the surgical sterilisation of the ‘mentally
deficient’ is in full swing. Over the previous decade, thousands of people have already been
sterilised across various US states, under laws penned and promoted by eugenics campaigners.
Inspired, Britain’s Eugenics Society — whose 700-strong membership included medical doctors,
clergymen and leading scientists, such as the statistician R A Fisher and the biologist Julian
Huxley — is on the march, pumping out propaganda pamphlets and filling correspondence
sections of UK newspapers, magazines and medical journals. Eugenic sterilisation, they argue,
is safe, humane, and urgently necessary. Only decisive action can curtail the supposed
overzealous breeding of so-called ‘defectives’ and arrest the racial deterioration of the British
people. Moreover, and crucially amid the economic wreckage of the Great Depression, a
sterilisation programme promises to curb the spiralling costs of caring for those deemed
‘feebleminded’ in overburdened state institutions.
Historians know what happens next, or rather, what doesn’t. Unlike their counterparts in the
United States, Canada or, notoriously, Germany, British politicians proved unwilling to ratify
such extreme and targeted interventions into the lives and bodies of individual citizens. When
introduced into Parliament in the summer of 1931, the Eugenics Society-backed Sterilisation
Bill was defeated — 89 ‘ayes’ versus 167 ‘noes’ (130 of which came from Labour MPs who
opposed the Bill as anti-working class). The matter was never again put to the vote in
Westminster. A near miss. Fast-forward a decade and a half and, amid the fallout from the
Second World War and revelations of Nazi genocide, ‘eugenics’ would acquire toxic political
baggage. The Eugenics Society limped on through the postwar period but, as the credibility of
the wider movement crumbled, its mission necessarily evolved. [Word Count: 358]

appear “non-masculine” — usually for the purpose of attracting women. Is picking up the

IV.	Many Years Later as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendia was to remember
that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice. At that time Macondo was a
village of twenty adobe houses, built on the bank of a river of clear water that ran along a bed
of polished stones, which were white and enormous, like prehistoric eggs. The world was so
recent that many things lacked names, and in order to indicate them it was necessary to point.
Every year during the month of March a family of ragged gypsies would set up their tents near
the village, and with a great uproar of pipes and kettledrums they would display new
inventions. First they brought the magnet. A heavy gypsy with an untamed beard and sparrow
hands, who introduced himself as Melquiades, put on a bold public demonstration of what he
himself called the eighth wonder of the learned alchemists of Macedonia. He went from house
to house dragging two metal ingots and everybody was amazed to see pots, pans, tongs, and
braziers tumble down from their places and beams creak from the desperation of nails and
screws trying to emerge, and even objects that had been lost for a long time appeared from
where they had been searched for most and went dragging along in turbulent confusion behind
Melquiades’ magical irons. “Things have a life of their own,” the gypsy proclaimed with a harsh
accent. “It’s simply a matter of waking up their souls.” José Arcadio Buendia, whose unbridled
imagination always went beyond the genius of nature and even beyond miracles and magic,
thought that it would be possible to make use of that useless invention to extract gold from the
bowels of the earth. Melquiades, who was an honest man, warned him: “It won’t work for that.”
But José Arcadio Buendia at that time did not believe in the honesty of gypsies, so he traded
his mule and a pair of goats for the two magnetized ingots. Ursula Iguaran, his wife, who
relied on those animals to increase their poor domestic holdings, was unable to dissuade him.
“Very soon we'll have gold, enough and more to pave the floors of the house,” her husband
replied. For several months he worked hard to demonstrate the truth of his idea. He explored
every inch of the region, even the riverbed, dragging the two iron ingots along and reciting
Melquiades’ incantation aloud. [Word Count: 407]

xX.	A contract of indemnity is a contract of protection by which one party undertakes to save the
other from loss. Halsbury describes indemnity as a contract, express or implied, to keep a
person indemnified against loss, independent of whether a third person makes default. Black’s
Law Dictionary also explains indemnity as a right by which the entire loss is shifted from one
who is only technically or secondarily liable to another who is primarily responsible. The
Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines it in Section 124 as a contract by which one party promises
to save the other from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or by the conduct of
any other person. The person giving the indemnity is the indemnifier, and the person
protected is the indemnity-holder or indemnified. The contract may be express or implied, as
seen in Adamson v. Jarvis, Secretary of State v. Bank of India Ltd., and Starkey v. Bank of
England, where courts recognised implied promises of indemnity from the circumstances and
conduct of parties.
The essential features of a contract of indemnity are that it must be a valid contract under the
Indian Contract Act, its main object must be protection from loss, its terms may be express or
implied, and it involves only two parties, unlike a contract of guarantee. It is contingent in
nature because liability arises on the happening of a specified event causing loss. Insurance
contracts are generally contracts of indemnity except life insurance, because life insurance
does not depend on proof of an actual quantified loss. As held in New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
v. State Trading Corporation of India, almost all insurance other than life and personal
accident insurance are contracts of indemnity. A third party cannot sue the indemnifier
because of the doctrine of privity, as observed in National Petroleum Company v. Popat Lal
Mulji.
Section 125 sets out the rights of the indemnity-holder. He may recover all damages he is
compelled to pay in a suit to which the indemnity applies, all costs incurred in bringing or
defending such a suit if he acted prudently and within authority, and all sums paid under a
reasonable compromise made in good faith. The indemnifier, though not expressly given rights
in the Act, enjoys subrogation rights after making payment. In Gajanan Moreshwar v.
Moreshwar Madan, the Bombay High Court held that once the indemnified’s liability becomes
absolute, the indemnifier must fulfil the promise without waiting for actual payment. This
modern rule departs from the old English view that actual loss must first be suffered. Cases
like Osman Jamal and Sons Ltd. v. Gopal Purushottam and The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
v. State Trading Corporation of India Ltd. support the principle that indemnity becomes
enforceable as soon as liability becomes absolute. However, indemnity will not cover unlawful
or intentional wrongful acts, as shown in Sheikh Meherulla v. Sariatulla and Geismar v. Sun
Alliance and London Insurance Ltd. Thus, contracts of indemnity remain an important legal
device for risk allocation, financial security, and protection against liability.

XI.	Belligerent occupation refers to a situation in which the armed forces of one state seize and
administer control over the territory of another sovereign state during armed conflict or its
aftermath. The control is not meant to be permanent; rather, it is provisional and continues
only for the period of military necessity or until the conflict is resolved. A territory is
considered under belligerent occupation when it is under the effective control of a hostile
army, meaning there must be actual administration and “boots on the ground,” and when the

XII. The doctrine of jus necessitatis, or necessity, has deep historical roots and recognises that in
certain exceptional situations, an act which would otherwise be unlawful may be justified if it
is done to prevent a greater harm. Medieval jurists such as Henry de Bracton stated that “that
which is otherwise not lawful is made lawful by necessity,” and Roman law reflected the same
idea in the maxim “Necessitas non habet legem’, meaning necessity knows no law. The
doctrine therefore developed as a legal justification for urgent acts done for survival,
preservation, or prevention of serious harm. In modern terms, jus necessitatis means a person
may do something technically illegal if it is necessary to avoid a more serious injury or danger.

In common law, the doctrine of necessity is mainly used as a defence, especially in criminal
law, though it has also appeared in administrative and constitutional law. It is supported by
the maxims “Quod necessitas non habet legem” and “Necessitas vincit legem”, the latter
meaning necessity triumphs over law. In India, the doctrine is codified in Section 81 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860, which states that an act likely to cause harm is not an offence if it is
done without criminal intention, in good faith, and for the purpose of preventing or avoiding
other harm to person or property. This Section 81 requires two essential conditions: absence of
criminal intent and good faith, along with the idea that the harm prevented must be greater
than the harm caused. For example, destroying one house to stop a fire from spreading to an
entire neighbourhood may be justified under Section 81.
Indian courts have recognised this doctrine in cases such as Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v.
APSRTC (1958) and Election Commission of India v. Dr. Subramaniam Swamy (1996), the
latter stressing that the doctrine should apply only in cases of absolute necessity.
International cases also illustrate its limits. In Regina v. Dudley and Stephens (1884),
necessity was rejected as a defence to murder, while United States v. Holmes (1842) and Rex
v. Bourne (1938) show that it may apply under strict conditions. The doctrine, however, is
limited by requirements of proportionality, good faith, absence of alternatives, and absolute
necessity. Though criticised for possible misuse, ambiguity, and erosion of legal certainty, it
remains an important legal principle for dealing with extraordinary situations where rigid
obedience to law would produce greater injustice.

XI. The Principles of Natural Justice are fundamental legal doctrines that ensure fairness,
impartiality, and reasoned decision-making in judicial, quasi-judicial, and administrative
proceedings. Rooted in moral principles, Roman law, and common law traditions, they protect
individuals from arbitrary action by requiring due process in decision-making. Their historical
basis can be traced to ancient Greek and Roman thought, medieval jurists such as Henry de
Bracton, and even religious narratives that emphasised giving a person an opportunity to explain
before punishment. In modern Indian law, the Supreme Court in Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief
Election Commissioner affirmed that fairness is essential in all forms of state decision-making. The
three core principles of natural justice are the hearing rule (audi alteram partem), the bias rule
(nemo judex in causa sua), and the requirement of a reasoned decision or speaking order.

The first principle, audi alteram partem, means that no person should be condemned without being
given a fair opportunity to be heard. It requires proper notice, a chance to present evidence and
arguments, the opportunity to cross-examine where necessary, and adjudication by an unbiased
authority. The second principle, nemo judex in causa sua, ensures that no one should be a judge in
their own cause. This rule guards against different forms of bias such as personal bias, pecuniary
bias, subject matter bias, departmental bias, policy notion bias, and bias due to stubbornness. The
third principle requires that every decision must be supported by reasons. A speaking order
promotes transparency, prevents arbitrariness, enables appeal or judicial review, and strengthens
accountability. These principles have become vital in administrative law, especially after Maneka
Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Supreme Court emphasised that fairness,
reasonableness, and justice are essential in procedures affecting rights and liberties.
Although natural justice is fundamental, it is not absolute and admits certain exceptions. It may be
excluded or modified in emergency situations, where immediate action is necessary for public
safety; by express statutory exclusion, where legislation validly limits procedural safeguards;
where disclosure would prejudice public interest, such as matters of national security; where
prompt action is needed; or where it is impracticable to hold a hearing or appeal. It may also be
relaxed in purely administrative matters, where no substantial legal right is affected, or where no
right of the person is infringed. Courts may also overlook procedural defects if they would have
made no difference to the outcome, or where the decision-maker acted in good faith without fault.
Even in such cases, however, these exceptions must be applied cautiously so that fairness,
transparency, and the protection of individual rights remain central to the legal process.
